title: Distinguishing descriptive from inferential statistics in retail analytics
scenario_markdown:
A national retail apparel chain evaluates two different analytics projects:
- **Project A (Chain-wide financial audit)**: The finance department aggregates total revenue, calculates the exact mean gross margin, and creates visual bar charts across all $120$ operating company stores for the past fiscal year using the verified corporate enterprise ledger.
- **Project B (Customer shopping experience study)**: The operations team randomly selects $40$ of the $120$ stores, records customer dwell time (minutes spent shopping) for $25$ shoppers at each sampled location, and computes a $95\%$ confidence interval to estimate the chain-wide average shopping duration.

parameters.objective: Classify business analytics tasks as descriptive or inferential statistics

assumptions: Project A examines a complete census of all 120 operating locations with complete transaction data
Project B draws an empirical sample to make broader generalizations about the entire chain
Classifications follow standard introductory business statistics definitions
source_refs: Course Module 1: Descriptive Measures & Basic Probability

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual definitions: Project A is descriptive statistics (census aggregation); Project B is inferential statistics (sample estimation under uncertainty). Stage 3 covers presence vs absence of sampling error.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should Project A (the financial audit of all $120$ stores) be classified, and why?

options.text_markdown: Descriptive statistics: It organizes, summarizes, and presents characteristics of a complete population (census) without estimating unknown parameters.
Inferential statistics: Because it involves calculating mathematical averages and totals across multiple stores.
options.hint_markdown: Computing a mean is descriptive when it summarizes complete data. Inferential statistics specifically refers to generalizing from a sample to an unseen population.

options.text_markdown: Predictive modeling: Because past financial data will be reviewed by company executives.
options.hint_markdown: Summarizing historical fiscal records describes what already occurred; it does not fit a forecasting model.

stages.explanation_markdown: Project A represents descriptive statistics. It deals with numerical and graphical methods designed to summarize, organize, and simplify an existing, complete dataset. Because all $120$ stores are measured, the metrics calculated (mean margin, total revenue) are exact population parameters of that fiscal year, not sample estimates.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should Project B (the customer dwell time study) be classified, and why?

options.text_markdown: Inferential statistics: It uses data from a subset (sample) of stores to draw conclusions and estimate an unknown parameter for the broader population.
Descriptive statistics: Because it calculates a sample average dwell time across the observed shoppers.
options.hint_markdown: While sample means are descriptive of the sample, constructing a confidence interval to estimate the entire chain's mean is the hallmark of inferential statistics.

options.text_markdown: A census: Because $40$ stores is a substantial fraction of the total $120$ store chain.
options.hint_markdown: A census requires measuring $100\%$ of the population. Measuring a $40$-store subset is a sample.

stages.explanation_markdown: Project B represents inferential statistics. It collects empirical evidence from a sample ($40$ stores) in order to make inferences, test claims, or estimate properties of the larger population (the entire chain-wide customer base). The $95\%$ confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty inherent in generalizing from a sample to the unobserved population.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which statement correctly describes how sampling error and statistical uncertainty apply to Project A versus Project B?

options.text_markdown: Project A has zero sampling error because it measures the entire population; Project B inherently involves sampling error, which is formally quantified by the confidence interval.
Both projects have equal sampling error because financial ledgers can contain accounting discrepancies.
options.hint_markdown: Sampling error arises solely from observing a subset instead of the whole population. Measuring all $120$ stores eliminates sampling error entirely.

options.text_markdown: Neither project has sampling error because $n = 40$ satisfies the Central Limit Theorem ($n \ge 30$).
options.hint_markdown: The CLT ensures the sampling distribution is approximately normal, but sampling error remains positive for any sample ($n < N$).

stages.explanation_markdown: Sampling error occurs when a sample statistic differs from the population parameter solely because of chance variation in which units were selected. Because Project A inspects the complete census ($120$ of $120$), its sampling error is strictly zero. In contrast, Project B inspects only a sample, meaning its sample mean will fluctuate across samples; inferential methods explicitly model and bound this sampling error.
